issues.legal_issue: The phrase requiring similar circumstances applies to both the same accommodation and similar accommodation when historical rents are used to determine basic rent.
material_facts: A tenant applied for fixation of fair rent for a shop rented under an agreement.
The lower appellate court relied on a historical rent for the same premises to determine basic rent.
The parties disputed whether the words requiring similar circumstances applied only to similar accommodation or also to the same premises.
issues.conclusion: The requirement of similar circumstances qualifies both the same accommodation and similar accommodation. A historical rent can be used only if the relevant accommodation existed in similar circumstances during the historical period.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 4(2)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, the phrase “in similar circumstances” governs both “the same” and “similar accommodation.” The prevailing rent for the same premises or similar accommodation is a basis for basic rent only when the circumstances are similar. The Court approved Chanan Singh v. Sewa Ram, 68 Punjab Law Reporter 335.

predicates.rent_control_fair_rent_proceeding: A party seeks a determination of fair rent in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.historical_rent_used_as_comparator: The decision-maker relies on a rent prevailing during an earlier period for the same or similar accommodation.

issues.definition: When fair rent is determined using an earlier rent, that rent is a valid comparator only if the accommodation existed in similar circumstances.

issues.legal_issue: General growth in a town’s size or prosperity alone does not establish a change in circumstances that displaces historical rental comparators.
material_facts: The landlord argued that the town and the locality had improved after the historical period and that the premises had also been materially improved.
The Court distinguished development of the locality or substantial development of the premises from general growth in the size and prosperity of a town.
The lower appellate court found that the historical rent for the premises was established for similar circumstances, and the Supreme Court found no legal basis to disturb that finding.
issues.conclusion: Development of the locality, or appreciable and substantial development of the premises through alterations or new construction, can change the relevant circumstances. General growth in the size and prosperity of the town alone is insufficient to take the case outside the historical-rent method.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(2)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 requires comparison in similar circumstances. Following Chanan Singh v. Sewa Ram, 68 Punjab Law Reporter 335, a change from an undeveloped to a developed locality is a change in circumstances; substantial development of the premises can also be such a change. General growth in the size and prosperity of the town alone is not enough.

rule.if: rent_control_fair_rent_proceeding and townwide_growth_only and not locality_development and not substantial_premises_development

predicates.rent_control_fair_rent_proceeding: A party seeks a determination of fair rent in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.townwide_growth_only: The asserted change in circumstances is general growth in the town’s size or prosperity, without a distinct asserted change in the relevant locality or premises.
predicates.locality_development: The locality has changed in character through development.
predicates.substantial_premises_development: The premises have undergone appreciable and substantial development through alterations, additions, or new construction.

issues.definition: In a fair-rent proceeding, townwide growth alone does not displace historical comparison when the locality and premises have not independently undergone the relevant development.

issues.legal_issue: A supported factual finding establishing the historical rent and similar circumstances, with no legal infirmity, may be left undisturbed on appeal.
material_facts: The tenant applied for fair rent, and the Rent Controller found the evidence insufficient to determine basic rent and maintained the contractual rent with an addition for taxes.
The District Judge accepted evidence that the historical rent for the premises was established for similar circumstances and allowed an increase under the Act.
The High Court affirmed the District Judge’s determination, and the Supreme Court found no legal infirmity warranting interference.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court did not disturb the District Judge’s finding fixing fair rent on the historical rent established by the evidence and the applicable statutory increase.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(2)(a) and 4(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 governed the determination of basic rent and the permitted increase. The Court found no infirmity of law in the District Judge’s factual finding, as affirmed by the High Court, that the prevailing rent had been proved for similar circumstances.

predicates.appeal_from_fair_rent_determination: A party appeals from a determination of fair rent made in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.historical_rent_finding_has_evidentiary_: The lower court’s finding about the historical rent and the relevant circumstances is supported by evidence it accepted.
predicates.no_legal_infirmity_in_finding: The challenged finding contains no legal error warranting appellate interference.

issues.definition: On appeal from a fair-rent determination, a supported finding about historical rent and similar circumstances is left undisturbed if it has no legal infirmity.

issues.legal_issue: When the governing law does not specify when a newly fixed fair rent takes effect, special circumstances may justify making it effective from a date later than the application.
material_facts: The Rent Controller maintained the contractual rent when the tenant applied for fair rent.
The District Judge first fixed fair rent in the appellate order.
The governing provision did not specify the commencement date, and the Supreme Court considered the circumstances sufficient to make the appellate order date the effective date.
issues.conclusion: The fair rent fixed by the District Judge was made effective from the date of the District Judge’s appellate order rather than from the date of the application.
issues.legal_principle: Although section 4 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 does not specify the date from which fixed fair rent takes effect, the ordinary starting point is the application date. The Court held that circumstances may justify another date and, in this case, selected the date of the appellate order because the Rent Controller had maintained the agreed rent and the appellate court had fixed fair rent.

rule.if: fair_rent_fixation_proceeding and governing_law_is_silent_on_start_date and controller_maintained_agreed_rent and appellate_court_first_fixed_fair_rent and special_circumstances_justify_later_effect

predicates.fair_rent_fixation_proceeding: A party seeks a determination of fair rent in a rent-control proceeding.
predicates.governing_law_is_silent_on_start_date: The governing law does not specify when the fixed fair rent begins to apply.
predicates.controller_maintained_agreed_rent: The first-instance rent decision maintained the rent agreed by the parties.
predicates.appellate_court_first_fixed_fair_rent: The appellate court was the first court to fix fair rent.
predicates.special_circumstances_justify_later_effe: The circumstances of the proceeding justify a commencement date later than the application date.

issues.definition: When the governing law is silent on commencement and the first-instance decision maintains the agreed rent while the appellate court first fixes fair rent, special circumstances may make the appellate fixation order the starting point.
